    loc_nr <- ( length(lon_field) * (loc_lat_idx - 1) ) + loc_lon_idx
} else { next()}

    if(all(is.na(tann_site))){  
        ctrl <- FALSE
        cnt <- 0
        distance <- array(NA, dim = c(3,9))
        for(j in c(-1,0,1)){
            for(k in c(-1,0,1)){
                tann_site <- tann_v1.2[loc_lon_idx+j,loc_lat_idx+k,]        
                if(all(!is.na(tann_site)) & sum(tann_site) != 0){

                    lat_temp <- lat_v1.2[loc_lat_idx+k]

                    cnt <- cnt + 1
                    distance[1,cnt] <- distance_temp
                    distance[2,cnt] <- j
                    distance[3,cnt] <- k
                }
            }
        }  
        
        j <- distance[2,which.min(distance[1,])]
        k <- distance[3,which.min(distance[1,])]
        loc_lon_idx <- loc_lon_idx+j
        loc_lat_idx <- loc_lat_idx+k
#         points(lon_v1.2[loc_lon_idx],lat_v1.2[loc_lat_idx], pch = 16)
        loc_nr <- (loc_lat_idx-1)*length(lon_field) + loc_lon_idx
        tann_site <- tann_v1.2[loc_lon_idx,loc_lat_idx,]
        pann_site <- pann_v1.2[loc_lon_idx,loc_lat_idx,] 
    }
    normparameter1 <- fitdistr(tann_site, "normal")
    normparameter2 <- fitdistr(pann_site, "normal")

speleo.check <- which( distances <= 150 )
skip <- FALSE

if( length(speleo.check) > 1 ){
    # search the best combination of age resolution and age range
    mean <- included.ages <- c()
    for(i in 1:length(speleo.check)){
        mean[i] <- mean( diff( d18o.age$age[[speleo.check[i]]] ), na.rm=T ) # age resolution
        included.ages[i] <- length( which(inside.range( site.age ,range(d18o.age$age[[speleo.check[i]]]) )) ) / length(site.age) # age range
    }
#     mean <- mean/max(mean)
    
    # note in sources

    pareto.df <- data.frame(mean,included.ages,distances[speleo.check])
    colnames(pareto.df) <- c("mean", "included.ages", "distance")
    # best combination pareto
    pareto.member <- psel(pareto.df, low(mean) * high(included.ages)* low(distance)) 

    max.included <- which.max(pareto.member$included.ages)
    which.site <- speleo.check[as.integer(rownames(pareto.member[max.included,])) ]

# make the climate prior more uninformative (increase of variance) if the recent age lies in younger holocene
if( recent & min(age) >= 2000 ){
    prior.recent$sd.pann <- prior.recent$sd.pann*2
    prior.recent$sd.tmp <- prior.recent$sd.tmp*2
}

# For large shape parameter the gamma distribution converges to normal distribution with mean μ = shape/rate and variance σ^2 = shape/(rate)^2
shape1 <- seq(0.1,50000,by=0.1)
rate1 <- shape1/prior.recent$mean.pann # includes the expectation value
rate2 <- sqrt(shape1)/prior.recent$sd.pann # includes the standard deviation

# plot(shape1,rate1,ty="l")
# lines(shape1,rate2)
# abline(v=shape1[which.min(abs((rate2-rate1) - 0))])

# intersection of rate1 and rate2
intersect_id <- which.min(abs((rate2-rate1) - 0))
shape <- shape1[intersect_id] 
rate  <- rate2[intersect_id]

# set.seed(2022)

# via interquantile range
# tann
set.seed(2022)
prior_tann_sample <- rnorm(10000,prior.recent$mean.tmp,prior.recent$sd.tmp)
tann_thresh <- quantile(prior_tann_sample,c(0.25,0.75))
# pann
set.seed(2022)
prior_pann_sample <- rgamma(10000,shape=shape,rate=rate)
pann_thresh <- quantile(prior_pann_sample,c(0.25,0.75))

# recent climate start values
if(recent){
    posterior$post_tann[1] <- prior.recent$mean.tmp - prior.recent$sd.tmp +rbeta(1,0.1,20) #rnorm(1,prior.recent$mean.tmp,5)
#     shape <- 20
    rate <- shape/prior.recent$mean.pann
    posterior$post_pann[1] <- prior.recent$mean.pann + prior.recent$sd.pann +rbeta(1,0.1,20) # rgamma(1,shape=shape,rate=rate)
stop()

    coi_array <- array(1, dim = dim(wt(df_speleo, s0 = s0, dj = 1/12, max.scale = max.scale, do.sig = FALSE)$power))

    if(recent){

In 2010 AD, a sediment composite core of $17,8\,$m was recovered during a drilling campaign in the Sea of Galilee.
The corresponding vegetational data are described in \cite{schiebel2018} and covers approximately the last 9,000 years.
Later, this palynological dataset was supplemented by additional samples to increase the temporal resolution (Thomas Litt, and Andrea Miebach, personal communucation).
During the reconstruction process, the Koeppen-Geiger classification shown in Fig. \ref{fig:kinneret_diagram}, is used as an anchor for the most recent time slice.
The problem of increasing human influence after about 6.5 cal ka BP is treated in the same way as for the Dead Sea in Sect. \ref{sec:dead_sea}. \par
Several references were used for the reconstructions of the Dead Sea region.
On the one hand, we include \acrshort{ap}/\acrshort{nap} from the core and isotope data from Soreq Cave for a reconstruction during the Holocene.
On the other hand, the \acrshort{ap}/\acrshort{nap} curve was replaced by isotopic information from the Mediterranean Sea (\acrshort{medstack}) for the period from the Penultimate to the Last Glacial.
Now all three proxy information are included, which are shown in Fig. \ref{fig:kinneret_reference}. \par
The Bayesian age-depth model of this sediment core is presented in more detail in \cite{miebach2022}.
It mainly includes \ce{^{14}C} measurements from terrestrial plants, sedimentary charcoal remains, and reservoir-corrected data from bulk sediments.

\subsubsection{Summary and conclusion}
The quantitative climate reconstruction of the Lake Kinneret region during the Holocene includes not only plant data, 
but also isotopic information from Soreq Cave and the Mediterranean Sea.
In the period before 6.6 cal ka BP, the reconstructed climate variables reflect the qualitative climate reconstructions explained in \cite{schiebel2018} and \cite{miebach2022}.
Although the final reconstruction is based only on isotopic information from speleothems and the Mediterranean Sea for ages younger than 6.5 cal ka BP, 
the results of \acrshort{pann} are comparable to the lake level of the Sea of Galilee \parencite{hazan2005}.
Moreover, the algorithm is able to find climate changes that can be associated with

The \acrshort{ap}/\acrshort{nap} reference curve in Fig. \ref{fig:gedi_reference} (a) also reveals this information.
For this reason, we include another climate proxy, isotopic data of speleothems from the nearby Soreq Cave (see Fig. \ref{fig:gedi_reference} (b)).
In Sect. \ref{sec:speleothems}, the description of these data are linked to precipitation in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Although the temporal space of this reference could be used for most periods of the Holocene \parencite{bar2007,bar2011}, we choose to use the pattern correlation of the respective \acrshort{wps}s.
% Although this reference could be used for most periods during the Holocene in temporal space \parencite{bar2007,bar2011}, we choose the pattern correlation of the respective \acrshort{wps}s.
This is due to the fact that the signal also reflects the composition of the source water of the Mediterranean Sea \parencite{litt2012}.
In this case, correlation in temporal space poses some problems, but moving to the appropriate spectral space allows us to circumvent them and take advantage of the variability within these data.
% Moreover, it is much more difficult for ancient humans to influence the signal in speleothems.
For all reconstructions within the Holocene and Levant, we choose the period $0-6.5$ cal ka BP as a zone of non-negligible human impact \parencite{schiebel2013}.
To account for this, the \acrshort{ap}/\acrshort{nap} curve is used as a guide to annual precipitation only for ages prior to 6.5 cal ka BP.
In contrast, this climate variable is correlated with patterns of the \acrshort{wps} from the Soreq Cave throughout the reconstruction period.\par
